title: Knowledge Check 10: Lessons 73-80
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 73-80 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why is cost per completed task a better metric to manage than cost per token?
options: Per-token prices fall while total bills rise, because work per task grows faster and hidden retries stay invisible
Per-token pricing is never published by providers at all, so the figure cannot be reconciled against a monthly invoice or used in a forecast
Per-token cost counts only generated output and ignores every input token the agent sends
Per-token cost is always the higher figure, so finance has more room to negotiate a lower contract
questions.explanation: A task bill grows even as unit prices fall, because the work one task performs multiplies across planning, tool calls, retries, and sub-agents. Cost per completed task captures that real spend, while cost per token hides it.

questions.question: A change cuts the context sent on each call but causes noticeably more model calls. Under the three-lever cost identity, what is the likely result?
options: It always saves money because context size is the only lever that reduces total cost directly, with no downside at all
It always loses money because any extra call doubles the effective per-token price of the task
The saving on context size can be spent back on call count, because the two multiply toward break-even
It has no cost effect because output cost is independent of both context size and call count
questions.explanation: Total cost is a product of three levers: context size, call count, and effective per-token price. A gain on one lever that spends on another can cancel out, so optimizations must be judged against all three at once.

questions.question: A team weighs moving a high-volume workload from a managed model API to self-hosted GPUs. What rule should decide it?
options: Self-host whenever the task is narrow, regardless of how heavily the purchased hardware is actually used
Stay on the managed API always, because per-token prices fall faster than hardware costs
Choose based on enthusiasm for open-weight models rather than on measured consumption
Move it only once sustained utilization clears the crossover, since idle GPUs are billed anyway
questions.explanation: Managed APIs price per token with no idle cost, while self-hosting shifts to fixed hourly cost that is wasteful when idle and efficient only at high utilization. The decision follows the crossover against measured utilization.

questions.question: Why does an agent security review start by naming assets and never-boundaries before listing attacks?
options: Because the attack list is identical for every agent and needs no local context to apply
Because you cannot decide what to defend against until you have named what a threat is meant to reach
Because threat modeling only ever cares about the confidentiality of stored customer records and nothing else
Because naming assets matters only for auditors after launch, not for the design itself
questions.explanation: You cannot harden against a threat until you know what it is trying to reach. Naming assets and the action the system must never take gives each threat something concrete to attach to.

questions.question: An injected instruction convinces the model to request a sensitive action. What actually prevents the action?
options: The model's safety training recognizes the injected text and refuses to proceed with the requested call
The retrieved document is validated and removed before it can enter the context window
A deterministic boundary the model cannot override makes the action unachievable from where it sits
The prompt is compared against a known-good hash and replaced whenever it has changed
questions.explanation: An injection targets the model, so moving its intent is not the same as moving the action. The defense lives in deterministic boundaries, such as permission limits and verify steps, that the model cannot talk its way past.

questions.question: What is the most important property of the residual-risk record in a written security review?
options: Every accepted risk carries a named owner and a reason, so it is a decision, not an omission
Every threat is fully mitigated so that no residual risk remains anywhere in the reviewed system
Residual risk is recorded only for threats that exceed a fixed token-spend threshold set by finance
The column is populated automatically by the vendor's security scanning tool at deployment time
questions.explanation: No agent is fully hardened, so the review must record which remaining risks were knowingly accepted and by whom. An accepted risk with a name and a reason is a decision; without one it is just an omission.

questions.question: Before rolling back or restarting an agent after confirming an incident, what must happen first?
options: Delete the affected session logs so that the bad behavior is not preserved in long-term storage
Revert to the last known-good prompt so the agent stops taking harmful actions
Export or snapshot the incident window's trace to storage independent of production
Restart the agent to clear its in-memory state before the investigation begins
questions.explanation: Recovery destroys evidence: a rollback swaps the running version and a restart clears in-memory state. The trace must be frozen to independent storage before any recovery action, or the record of what happened is lost.

questions.question: A sent customer message later turns out to be wrong. How does rollback by action class treat this case?
options: It cannot be unsent, so the response is a corrective follow-up plus an impacted-customer list
It is idempotent like a database write, so it can be reversed with a standard transactional rollback
It can be recalled because the agent still holds read access to the customer inbox
It can be ignored once the agent is restarted and the message becomes untraceable
questions.explanation: Some actions cannot be reversed, only compensated. A message already sent cannot be unsent, so the substitute is a follow-up correction and the list of customers affected, not a revert.

questions.question: In a detection chain from harmful action to human acknowledgement, what does a delay between the signal firing and the tripwire tripping point to?
options: Missing instrumentation on the path where the agent took its action
A tripwire that never fired and therefore needs to be built or repaired
Poor alerting hygiene, because the page never actually reached a human on call
A slow human response after the page was received and acknowledged
questions.explanation: Each gap in the detection chain has its own root cause. A delay between signal and trigger means a tripwire that should have fired did not, so the fix is the missing or broken tripwire.

questions.question: An operator plans to reproduce a past agent run by setting temperature to zero and re-running it. Why does this fail?
options: Sampling is only one step, and the logits that feed it are not bit-identical run to run
Temperature zero disables all tool calls, so the re-run halts on its first tool invocation immediately
Setting temperature to zero stops trace capture, so nothing is recorded on the re-run
Every inference provider forbids temperature zero for agent workloads in production
questions.explanation: Temperature controls only the sampling step, while the logits behind it vary with batch composition and hardware numerics. A run therefore cannot be reproduced by running it again; it must be reconstructed from the record.

questions.question: How does deterministic replay reconstruct a past agent run?
options: It re-runs the agent live against current models and compares the new output
It feeds the recorded interactions back in sequence, with stubs replacing live calls
It relies on the model provider's cache to return the same tokens when given the same prompt again
It lowers the sampling temperature until the model stabilizes on a single answer
questions.explanation: Replay does not re-invoke the model or tools. It substitutes proxy stubs that return the recorded responses in the exact original sequence, turning the log into a reproducible witness.

questions.question: How do you prove that an exported agent trace was not altered since it was written?
options: Replay the run live and show that the current output matches the original output
Trust the log because it lives on an append-only store that the agent itself can never rewrite or alter
Ask the engineer who restored the system to confirm that nothing was changed
Recompute the trace's message digest and compare it to the hash stored out of band at write time
questions.explanation: Integrity hashing records a digest of the trace when it is collected and stores it where it cannot change. Re-hashing later and matching proves the record is unaltered, since a single changed bit yields a different digest.

questions.question: When should a remote peer be reached over an agent-to-agent protocol rather than wrapped as a tool?
options: When the peer plans and loops on its own, so a durable task, cancellation, and input requests must survive
When the peer is a simple function that returns the same deterministic result for the same input
When both options use the same transport, so the choice reduces to picking fewer dependencies
When the client should import the peer's prompts and tool definitions directly so that its behavior stays consistent
questions.explanation: The deciding question is what sits on the far side of the boundary. A deterministic function can be a tool, but an agent that plans and loops needs an agent boundary that preserves the durable task and its states.

questions.question: A peer returns a state indicating it needs more input before it can continue. What is the correct client behavior?
options: Treat it as a failure and open a brand new task with a fresh message id
Poll the task endpoint without limit until the state becomes completed
Supply the missing information in another message bound to the same task id
Cancel the task entirely and retry the whole request later with a different payload and message id
questions.explanation: An input-required state is interrupted, not failed. The task id stays alive, so the client supplies the missing information on the same task instead of stranding or duplicating the work.

questions.question: An agent loads a peer's published capability card and its skill examples into its own context. What stance is correct?
options: The card is authoritative, so a declared capability is enough authorization to delegate
A valid signature proves the peer is trustworthy, so its returned outputs need no further validation on your side at all
The card can be ignored at runtime because the version changes too often to check
The card is a claim from a stranger: verify capabilities at runtime and treat its text as untrusted data
questions.explanation: A card is an advertisement written by the party asking for work, and its free-form text becomes part of a prompt. A signature only proves origin, so delegation should follow your own policy and the card text should be treated as untrusted.

questions.question: A process has steps you can enumerate, a bounded step count, and a validator that can judge each step's output. Which shape fits?
options: An autonomous agent, because the number of items varies from batch to batch
An orchestrator that discovers its own subtasks per run with no fixed outer structure
A workflow, because the steps are enumerable and code can gate whether each one succeeded
A workflow only if no model is used anywhere, since any model call would break determinism
questions.explanation: When code can name the steps and a validator can decide success, determinism is a feature. A model may still do real work inside a workflow, but it never chooses the next step.

questions.question: You place an agent as one step inside a durable workflow. What must the seam define before the first run?
options: Typed input and output schemas, validation, an idempotency key, a timeout, a cost ceiling, and an escalation
An unbounded iteration budget so that the agent can always finish, plus a logged transcript kept for audit purposes
Direct access to the workflow event history so the engine can replay the agent's reasoning later
A shared prompt registry so the deterministic engine can cache the model result on every replay
questions.explanation: The engine only sees the validated result or a failure it can route, so the seam needs explicit contracts. Every undefined item, from the idempotency key to the cost ceiling, becomes an incident later.

questions.question: Why must a model call never sit inside deterministic workflow code?
options: Because the model would cost more than a plain function call and inflate the overall run budget
Because the workflow is replayed to rebuild state, and a fresh model answer breaks that match
Because workflow engines cannot serialize a model response into their event history
Because the model needs network access, which the engine always blocks for security
questions.explanation: Durable workflow code is re-run to reconstruct state from the recorded history. A model call returns a different answer on replay, so the history no longer matches the code; the model belongs in an activity or step.

questions.question: Why should the classifier that decides which actions need approval be deterministic rather than a model reading the same content?
options: A model classifier is too slow to sit in a real-time approval path at scale
A model fed the same untrusted content can be talked into marking a request low-risk
A model cannot output a risk tier at all without being fine-tuned on past approvals
Running the classifier on a separate model from the agent removes any adversarial influence
questions.explanation: If the classifier reads the same untrusted text as the request, adversarial content can sway it. Deterministic policy logic should be the authoritative signal, with model-assisted classification only as optional input that a deterministic layer re-checks.

questions.question: An agent starts behaving anomalously and must be contained. In what order should the response proceed?
options: Stop the process, then page the team, then review the logs at leisure afterward
Revoke the credentials, then snapshot, then skip notifying dependents to avoid panic
Snapshot the state, revoke the credentials, then notify dependents so they can trip breakers
Pause new intake and then let in-flight tasks finish, since that on its own contains any anomaly
questions.explanation: Evidence first, then authority, then notification. Recovery destroys evidence, permissions are the real capability, and notifying dependents lets downstream workflows activate their circuit breakers.

questions.question: What makes an approval gate a real control rather than a suggestion?
options: It asks the agent to pause and wait until a reviewer sends a confirmation message
It routes absolutely every action through human review, so nothing can ever proceed without someone looking at it
It shows only the proposed action, keeping the reviewer's screen uncluttered and fast
Its approval releases the credential that performs the action, so the action cannot proceed without it
questions.explanation: A pause the workflow can route around is only a request. The gate must sit in the authorization path, where approval is what mints or releases the credential that performs the action.

questions.question: A company licenses a vendor's high-risk scoring engine, rebrands it under its own name, and puts it into service. What role does it now hold?
options: Deployer only, because the vendor developed the underlying model and carries every single obligation
Provider of that component, which pulls the full provider duty set onto the company
Neither provider nor deployer, because rebranding does not change any duty at all
Both roles in equal measure, so the company picks whichever duty set is cheaper
questions.explanation: Placing a high-risk system into service under your own name or trademark makes you its provider, not merely a deployer. That branding converts a limited deployer role into the full provider duty set.

questions.question: Why is how long agent traces are kept a design decision rather than a routine operations setting?
options: A plain-language explanation may be demanded weeks after a decision, so decision-time context must survive
Longer retention always lowers storage cost once the data has been compressed and archived
Regulators require every agent run to be kept for exactly one calendar year in all cases
Logs must always be deleted quickly to comply with data-minimization principles and reduce exposure to risk
questions.explanation: Some regimes require an explanation of an adverse decision well after the fact, and that needs the inputs, model version, and prompt version from decision time. Retention must be set against the longest applicable window.

questions.question: In the United States, which layer of AI rules actually binds a builder today?
options: A comprehensive federal statute that preempts all state and local AI rules
Voluntary federal frameworks, which are entirely optional in practice and carry no binding weight at all
State and city statutes, because there is no federal statute and an order cannot preempt them
A federal executive order, because it can override any conflicting state AI legislation
questions.explanation: There is no comprehensive federal statute, and an executive order cannot preempt a state law; that takes Congress or a valid regulation. Until then, state and city statutes are the binding layer to build against.
